title: Foreign buyers are the main reason house prices are out of reach
oneLiner: Overseas money bidding up Australian homes is blamed for the affordability gap.
body: Foreign purchasers, particularly in new apartment developments and prestige suburbs, are widely believed to be a major source of price pressure. Proponents argue that tightening foreign investment rules would do more for affordability than changing tax concessions for local investors.
contextBackground: Foreign buyers are already restricted to new dwellings and pay additional duties and fees. Their share of transactions, as reported by the foreign investment regulator, is small. The claim is nonetheless widely believed, which makes it useful to see how it rates.
contextDisagreement: Critics point to the regulator's own figures on the volume of approved foreign purchases and argue they are too small to drive a national market. Supporters argue the official figures understate purchases made through local intermediaries.

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.
